meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Nobody made a greater mistake than he who did nothing because he could do only a little'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Edmund Burke. The idea comes from Sydney Smith (1850); the famous wording is a modern paraphrase, and the Burke tag dates only to 1981.

answer.label: Not Edmund Burke — the thought is Sydney Smith's, the wording a later paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: There is no substantive evidence Edmund Burke ever said or wrote this, and the earliest attribution to him dates only to 1981. The idea comes from Rev. Sydney Smith’s “Elementary Sketches of Moral Philosophy” (published 1850, from lectures of 1804–1806), which reads “It is the greatest of all mistakes, to do nothing because you can only do little” — the modern “Nobody made a greater mistake…” wording is a paraphrase of Smith, not his exact words.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: It is the greatest of all mistakes, to do nothing because you can only do little: but there are men who are always clamouring for immediate and stupendous effects…
trail: Quote Investigator traces the earliest match to Sydney Smith’s 1850 Elementary Sketches of Moral Philosophy and finds no evidence Burke used the saying.
The Edmund Burke attribution is modern: QI’s earliest Burke ascription dates only to 1981, long after Burke’s 1797 death.
Smith’s original book is freely readable at the Internet Archive, where the lectures of 1804–1806 appear as published in 1850.
Even on quote aggregators the Burke version carries “attributed, no source” and “quote by Sydney Smith” tags.
source.excerptNote: Sydney Smith’s original wording in the 1850 text. The circulating “Nobody made a greater mistake than he who did nothing because he could do only a little” is a paraphrase of this passage — and is not found in Edmund Burke’s works at all.

source.rightsNote: The underlying idea comes from Sydney Smith’s Elementary Sketches of Moral Philosophy, first published in 1850 — a work now in the public domain. But the specific circulating wording (“Nobody made a greater mistake…”) is a later, anonymous paraphrase that matches neither Smith’s nor Burke’s exact text, so no clean rights status attaches to it as quoted.

author.heading: Sydney Smith, not Edmund Burke
author.metaLine: 1771–1845 · English clergyman, essayist & co-founder of the Edinburgh Review
author.bio: Sydney Smith was an English Anglican cleric, writer, and celebrated conversational wit, remembered as one of the founders of the Edinburgh Review in 1802. The line traces to his lectures on moral philosophy delivered at the Royal Institution in 1804–1806 and published posthumously in 1850, where he warned against the paralysis of doing nothing simply because one can do only a little.

misattribution.heading: A double error: wrong author, reworded words
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s classic feel-good misattributions. It is pinned on Edmund Burke — a magnet name — even though the idea belongs to Sydney Smith and the familiar phrasing belongs to neither man.

items.why: Quote Investigator located no substantive evidence that Burke ever used this saying; the earliest attribution to him appears only in 1981, in As Lambs To The Slaughter, nearly two centuries after his death in 1797.
The thought first appears in Smith’s Elementary Sketches of Moral Philosophy (1850): “It is the greatest of all mistakes, to do nothing because you can only do little.”
“Nobody made a greater mistake than he who did nothing because he could do only a little” is a modern rewrite of Smith’s sentence — the words are not a verbatim quotation of anyone.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest credit: the idea is Sydney Smith’s (1850), the popular wording is an anonymous paraphrase, and Edmund Burke has no documented claim to it at all.

context.heading: Why the line sticks to Burke
lead: Edmund Burke is a natural magnet for stirring political and civic aphorisms — he is already (wrongly) credited with “The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is that good men do nothing.” A quote about not letting the smallness of one’s contribution excuse inaction fits that same heroic register, so it drifted onto his name.
In reality the sentiment belongs to Sydney Smith, a clergyman famous for wit and common sense, delivered in lectures two centuries ago and softened into its current slogan form by later hands.
context.pull: The idea is Sydney Smith’s; the words are nobody’s in particular; the name is wrong.
